```{r}
#| label: tbl-regional-years
#| tbl-cap: "The regional predictions year by year, against the mean observed date. The intercepts of @tbl-regional are not applied here, so the columns differ by a constant"
reg_rows |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(localities = n(),
            `observed mean` = round(mean(obs_p50), 1),
            `BioSIM regional` = round(first(biosim_regional), 1),
            `BioSIM site mean` = round(mean(biosim_site), 1),
            `bayessbw regional` = round(first(bayes_regional), 1),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(Year = as.character(Year)) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Two caveats on the comparison. The regional predictors cannot capture real
site-to-site variation, because they are constant within a year — the result
is not that no such variation exists, but that it is smaller than the error
the models make when they try to represent it. And averaging temperature
before running a development model is not the same as averaging the
development of each site, since the rate curves are non-linear; the regional
bayessbw run is a model of the average weather, not an average of the models.

Taken with @sec-sync this is the practical conclusion of the comparison. For
predicting when spruce budworm flies in Maine, the useful signal in these
models is the year, not the site; and a phenology model applied at a single
trap's coordinates will be wrong by about six days, mostly because it imposes
a latitudinal gradient the moths do not follow. @sec-count turns that finding
into a predictive model and measures what it can do.

# Predicting the nightly catch curve {#sec-count}

```{r}
#| label: count-data
count_model <- readRDS(file.path("data", "processed", "nightly_count_model.rds"))
cnt_scores  <- count_model$scores
cnt_cv      <- count_model$cv
cnt_nights  <- count_model$nights
cnt_sum     <- count_model$summary

## Headline numbers for the prose. Inline `r` cannot carry escaped backticks,
## so anything needing a backticked column name is computed here.
cnt_best <- cnt_cv |>
  filter(model == "reg+") |>
  summarise(mae    = mean(abs(err_p50)),
            rmse   = sqrt(mean(err_p50^2)),
            bias   = mean(err_p50),
            within = mean(abs(err_p50) <= 5))

cnt_best_all <- cnt_cv |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(mae      = mean(abs(err_p50)),
            per_moth = sum(loglik * nights_n) / sum(total),
            .groups  = "drop")
```

Everything so far has compared summary dates. This section asks the
predictive question directly: given a development model, how well can the
**shape of a season** be predicted at a locality — the share of its catch
falling on each night?

Abundance is deliberately not predicted. Nothing in this project forecasts
population density, so every model below carries one free level per
locality-year that absorbs the season total and leaves only timing to
explain. A Poisson likelihood with such a level per group is a multinomial
over that group's nights, so the fitted values read directly as predicted
shares, and a held-out locality-year needs no level of its own.

`R/10_nightly_count_model.R` fits `r nrow(cnt_scores)` such models to
`r format(cnt_sum$n_nights, big.mark = ",")` trapped nights from
`r cnt_sum$n_ly` locality-years
(`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cnt_sum$zero_share)` of nights caught nothing) and
scores them leave-one-year-out.

| Model | What drives the shape |
|-------|-----------------------|
| `clim` | a seasonal curve only, `ns(day of year)` fitted from the other years — the climatological baseline any predictor must beat |
| `raw` | BioSIM's site curve used as is, no fitted parameters |
| `site` | the same curve with a free exponent |
| `site+` | plus a spline correction in days from the modelled median |
| `reg+` | the same, driven by one regional BioSIM curve per year |
| `reg+lat` | plus a latitude interaction |
| `pup+` | the same calibration applied to bayessbw's predicted pupation distribution instead of BioSIM's flight curve, locality by locality |
| `pupreg+` | and to one regional bayessbw run per year |
| `reg-med` | the regional curve stripped out entirely, leaving only the spline in days from its median: the development model contributes a date and nothing else |

: The nine specifications {#tbl-count-models}

The two bayessbw rows need no lag constant. The correction is a spline in days
from the driving curve's own median, so the interval between pupation and the
catch is fitted rather than assumed — which is what made the shifted series on
@fig-compare uninformative about level and is repaired here.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-count-scores
#| tbl-cap: "Leave-one-year-out skill. Log-likelihood is the multinomial log-likelihood of the observed counts given the predicted shares, reported per moth so that it reads as a mean log predicted share"
cnt_cv |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(`log-lik per moth` = sum(loglik * nights_n) / sum(total),
            `mean |p50 error|, d` = mean(abs(err_p50)),
            `RMSE p50, d` = sqrt(mean(err_p50^2)),
            `bias, d` = mean(err_p50),
            `within 5 d` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(abs(err_p50) <= 5)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = levels(cnt_scores$model))) |>
  arrange(model) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Four things come out of that table.


**A calibrated regional curve is the best predictor**, and it is a usable one:
`r sprintf("%.1f", cnt_best$mae)` days of mean absolute error on the median
catch date, a bias of `r sprintf("%+.1f", cnt_best$bias)` days, and
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cnt_best$within)` of locality-years inside five
days — all out of sample, and with no information from the year being
predicted.

**BioSIM's raw site curve does no better than climatology.** Used as
delivered it ties a seasonal average fitted from other years on mean absolute
error (4.47 d against 4.48 d) and is worse on the two metrics that penalise
large misses and mis-placed nightly mass: RMSE 5.82 d against 5.30 d, and a
mean log predicted share of −3.38 against −3.35. Its bias is the largest of
any specification at −2.19 d. Giving the curve a free exponent helps, a shape
correction does not, and replacing the site curve with the single regional one
helps most. Latitude makes things worse again, for the fourth time in this
log.

**The pupation distribution does not do better than the flight curve.**
Applied locality by locality it lands where BioSIM's site curve does
(`r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$mae[cnt_best_all$model == "pup+"])` days
against `r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$mae[cnt_best_all$model == "site+"])`),
and the regional bayessbw run is the weaker of the two
(`r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$mae[cnt_best_all$model == "pupreg+"])` days)
— the opposite of BioSIM, where going regional helped most. Both bayessbw
specifications are almost unbiased, which is the spline absorbing the
pupation-to-catch interval as intended, but they are less sharp: a mean log
predicted share of
`r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$per_moth[cnt_best_all$model == "pup+"])`
and `r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$per_moth[cnt_best_all$model == "pupreg+"])`
against `r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$per_moth[cnt_best_all$model == "reg+"])`
for the best. Two independent development models place pupation within a day
of each other, so this is not a disagreement about the date; it is that
bayessbw's year-to-year placement carries less of the signal the catches
follow, consistent with its weaker year-mean correlation in
@tbl-compare-structure.

**Almost all of the shape is empirical.** The fitted exponent on the regional
curve is `r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_sum$exponent)`, so the modelled curve enters
the prediction heavily damped. `reg-med` settles how much it is worth by
removing it altogether and keeping only the spline in days from its median:
that costs nothing on timing
(`r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$mae[cnt_best_all$model == "reg-med"])` days
of mean absolute error against
`r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$mae[cnt_best_all$model == "reg+"])`, the same
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(abs(cnt_cv$err_p50[cnt_cv$model == "reg-med"]) <= 5))`
inside five days) and a little on the nightly likelihood
(`r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$per_moth[cnt_best_all$model == "reg-med"])`
against `r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$per_moth[cnt_best_all$model == "reg+"])`
per moth). So what the development model contributes is *when* the season is
centred — which year runs early, which runs late — and the curve's own form
adds only a marginal sharpening of the nightly fit.

Measured on the trapped nights, where the fit is supported, the correction
moves the predicted median `r sprintf("%+.1f", cnt_sum$shift)` days relative
to BioSIM's curve as delivered, with a spread of
`r sprintf("%.1f", cnt_sum$shift_sd)` days across locality-years, and it
widens the predicted central 90% from
`r sprintf("%.1f", cnt_sum$raw_width)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", cnt_sum$cal_width)`
days. The observed central 90% is `r sprintf("%.1f", cnt_sum$obs_width)` days,
so the calibrated prediction is well centred and too broad. Part of that gap
is not model error: the observed width is one realisation of a very
overdispersed count and a spiky realisation is narrower than the mean curve
behind it. @sec-forecast measures it properly by simulating realisations, and
the over-width survives at about two and a half days rather than the five
this comparison suggests.

```{r}
#| label: fig-count-skill
#| fig-cap: "Out-of-sample prediction of the median catch date. Left: the calibrated regional model against the observed median, one point per locality-year, with the 1:1 line. Right: the distribution of signed errors for each specification; the box spans the quartiles, the line is the median, whiskers reach 1.5 times the interquartile range."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

best <- filter(cnt_cv, model == "reg+")
lims <- range(c(best$obs_p50, best$pred_p50))

p_pred <- ggplot(best, aes(obs_p50, pred_p50)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "22", colour = "grey45") +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7, colour = "#1f6f8b") +
  annotate("text", x = lims[2], y = lims[2], hjust = 1, vjust = 1.8,
           size = 3, colour = "grey45", label = "1:1") +
  coord_equal(xlim = lims, ylim = lims) +
  labs(title = "Held-out years are predicted to about three days",
       x = "Observed median catch date (DOY)",
       y = "Predicted median (DOY)")

ord <- cnt_scores$model
p_err <- cnt_cv |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = ord)) |>
  ggplot(aes(model, err_p50)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey45", linetype = "22") +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = model == "reg+"), width = 0.6, outlier.size = 0.7,
               linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#1f6f8b", `FALSE` = "grey85")) +
  labs(title = "and the regional curve beats the rest",
       x = NULL, y = "Predicted minus observed (d)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

base <- theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "plain", hjust = 0),
        legend.position = "none")

(p_pred & base) | (p_err & base + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-count-residual
#| tbl-cap: "Where the calibrated regional model still misses"
best_lat <- best |>
  left_join(distinct(cnt_nights, site_year, Latitude), by = "site_year")

tibble::tibble(
  Quantity = c("Mean |error|, southern localities (below 45.5 \u00b0N)",
               "Mean |error|, northern localities",
               "Error against latitude",
               "Error against log10 season total",
               "Worst locality-year"),
  Value = c(
    sprintf("%.2f d", mean(abs(best_lat$err_p50[best_lat$Latitude <  45.5]))),
    sprintf("%.2f d", mean(abs(best_lat$err_p50[best_lat$Latitude >= 45.5]))),
    sprintf("r = %+.2f", cor(best_lat$err_p50, best_lat$Latitude)),
    sprintf("r = %+.2f", cor(best_lat$err_p50, log10(best_lat$total))),
    with(best[which.max(abs(best$err_p50)), ],
         sprintf("%s %d, %+.1f d", sub(", Maine$", "", Location), Year, err_p50))
  )
) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r"))
```

Calibration removes most of the spatial structure: the residual's correlation
with latitude falls to
`r sprintf("%+.2f", cor(best_lat$err_p50, best_lat$Latitude))`
from the +0.49 of @sec-compare. A southern excess survives — mean absolute
error `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(abs(best_lat$err_p50[best_lat$Latitude < 45.5])))`
days against `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(abs(best_lat$err_p50[best_lat$Latitude >= 45.5])))`
in the north — so the gradient is corrected on average rather than explained.

## What this model is and is not good for

It predicts **timing**, out of sample, to about three days on the median and
within five days four times out of five. That is enough to say when a flight
season will be centred at a Maine locality given the year's weather, which is
the operational question. Its predicted **spread** is too wide by about half
again, so a prediction interval taken straight from the fitted curve will be
conservative.

It does not predict **how many** moths will be caught: the season total is an
input, not an output. It also does not separate flight from trappability.
Nightly weather is absent by design, and the model's own diagnostics show
where that would pay: `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cnt_sum$zero_share)` of nights
caught nothing, and the count variance is several thousand times the mean, so
the nightly residual is dominated by night-to-night variation that a
development model cannot address. Temperature, wind and precipitation at each
locality-night are already extracted and would enter this model as covariates
without changing anything else about it.

One technical caveat for anyone refitting: the correction spline is a natural
spline in days from the modelled median, and its behaviour beyond about
\u00b115 days rests on few nights — the upturn at the far right of the fitted
correction is an edge artefact, not a second flight period.

# What distribution describes a night's catch? {#sec-dist}

```{r}
#| label: dist-data
count_dist <- readRDS(file.path("data", "processed", "count_distribution.rds"))
dist_cmp   <- count_dist$comparison
dist_mv    <- count_dist$mv
dist_bands <- count_dist$band_table
dist_sum   <- count_dist$summary

dist_get <- function(fam, col) dist_cmp[[col]][dist_cmp$family == fam]
## Variance inflation each quadratic family implies at a given mean:
## nbinom2 has var = mu + mu^2/theta, the lognormal mixture
## var = mu + mu^2 (exp(sigma^2) - 1).
nb2_factor <- 1 / dist_get("nbinom2", "dispersion")
pln_factor <- exp(dist_sum$nightly_sd^2) - 1
```

The marginal distribution of nightly counts is not a useful target: these
nights differ enormously in what they should hold, from a locality-year
totalling a hundred moths to one totalling seventy thousand, and within a
season from the first night of flight to the peak. The question worth asking
is conditional — **given what a night is expected to hold, how is the count
scattered around it?**

`R/11_count_distribution.R` gives every candidate the same mean structure, the
`reg+` predictor of @sec-count with a locality-year level, and varies only the
distribution of the count around that mean.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dist
#| tbl-cap: "Conditional distributions for a night's catch, same mean structure throughout. Zero-catch nights and the largest count are posterior predictive checks: the median over 100 simulations from each fitted model"
## Column names are set afterwards: R does not accept \u escapes inside
## backtick-quoted names.
dist_cmp |>
  transmute(family, parameters, AIC = round(AIC), dAIC = round(dAIC),
            zeros = round(zeros_simulated),
            largest = format(round(max_simulated), big.mark = ",")) |>
  setNames(c("Family", "par", "AIC", "\u0394AIC", "zero nights",
             "largest count")) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Observed: **`r format(dist_sum$zeros_observed, big.mark = ",")` zero-catch
nights** of `r format(dist_sum$n_nights, big.mark = ",")`, and a largest count
of `r format(dist_sum$max_observed, big.mark = ",")` moths.

**The Poisson is hopeless**, by
`r format(round(dist_get("poisson", "dAIC")), big.mark = ",")` AIC. It expects
`r round(dist_get("poisson", "zeros_simulated"))` empty nights where
`r format(dist_sum$zeros_observed, big.mark = ",")` occurred. The raw
variance-to-mean ratio of the catches is
`r format(round(dist_sum$var_ratio), big.mark = ",")`.

**Zero inflation is unnecessary.** Adding a zero-inflation component to the
negative binomial costs two AIC and moves nothing — the fitted component is
essentially empty, and the simulated number of empty nights is unchanged. The
empty nights are the lower tail of a very overdispersed count distribution,
not a separate process that switches the trap off. That is worth stating
plainly, because a zero-inflated model is the reflex for trap data with a
quarter of its nights empty.

**The variance is quadratic in the mean, and the negative binomial has it
right.** Binning nights by their expected catch gives an empirical
variance-mean slope of `r sprintf("%.2f", dist_sum$mv_slope)` on the log
scale, where 1 is the Poisson and `nbinom1` and 2 is the negative binomial
(NB2). `nbinom1`, which forces slope 1, is beaten by
`r format(round(dist_get("nbinom1", "dAIC")), big.mark = ",")` AIC, and NB2's
fitted variance function tracks the binned data across three orders of
magnitude (@fig-dist).

```{r}
#| label: fig-dist
#| fig-cap: "Left: variance against expected catch for nights binned into twenty groups, with the variance function each family assumes. Points are binned on the negative binomial's fitted mean, which conditions on the locality-year level only; binning on the Poisson-lognormal's fitted values would condition on its nightly random effect and collapse the points onto the Poisson line. Right: the share of nights in each count band, observed and simulated from each fitted model."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

fam_cols <- c(Poisson = "grey60", nbinom1 = "#8c6d31",
              nbinom2 = "#1f6f8b", `Poisson-lognormal` = "#d1670f")

mu_grid <- exp(seq(log(min(dist_mv$mean_mu)), log(max(dist_mv$mean_mu)),
                   length.out = 100))
curves <- bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(family = "Poisson", mu = mu_grid, v = mu_grid),
  tibble::tibble(family = "nbinom1", mu = mu_grid,
                 v = mu_grid * (1 + dist_get("nbinom1", "dispersion"))),
  tibble::tibble(family = "nbinom2", mu = mu_grid,
                 v = mu_grid + mu_grid^2 * nb2_factor),
  tibble::tibble(family = "Poisson-lognormal", mu = mu_grid,
                 v = mu_grid + mu_grid^2 * pln_factor)
) |>
  mutate(family = factor(family, levels = names(fam_cols)))

p_mv <- ggplot(dist_mv, aes(mean_mu, var_y)) +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(mu, v, colour = family), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.9, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = fam_cols) +
  labs(title = "The variance follows the negative binomial",
       x = "Expected catch of the night (moths)", y = "Variance of the count",
       colour = NULL)

p_band <- dist_bands |>
  filter(source %in% c("observed", "nbinom2", "poisson-ln")) |>
  mutate(source = recode(source, observed = "Observed", nbinom2 = "nbinom2",
                         `poisson-ln` = "Poisson-lognormal"),
         source = factor(source, levels = c("Observed", "nbinom2",
                                            "Poisson-lognormal"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(band, share, fill = source)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Observed = "grey30", nbinom2 = "#1f6f8b",
                               `Poisson-lognormal` = "#d1670f")) +
  labs(title = "and both families place the nights correctly",
       x = "Moths caught", y = "Share of nights", fill = NULL)

base <- theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "plain", hjust = 0),
        legend.key.size = unit(0.8, "lines"))

(p_mv & base + theme(legend.position = "inside",
                     legend.position.inside = c(0.02, 0.98),
                     legend.justification = c(0, 1),
                     legend.background = element_blank())) |
  (p_band & base + theme(legend.position = "bottom",
                         axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)))
```

**The Poisson-lognormal wins the likelihood but not the second moment.** A
Poisson count whose mean carries a lognormal nightly multiplier fits better by
`r round(dist_get("nbinom2", "dAIC"))` AIC and reproduces the number of empty
nights most closely
(`r round(dist_get("poisson-ln", "zeros_simulated"))` against
`r format(dist_sum$zeros_observed, big.mark = ",")`, where NB2 gives
`r round(dist_get("nbinom2", "zeros_simulated"))`). Its fitted multiplier has
a lognormal standard deviation of
`r sprintf("%.2f", dist_sum$nightly_sd)` on the log scale, which implies a
variance inflation of `r sprintf("%.0f", pln_factor)` times the squared mean
against the `r sprintf("%.1f", nb2_factor)` the data show — about
`r sprintf("%.0f", pln_factor / nb2_factor)` times too much. Its simulated
largest count is
`r format(round(dist_get("poisson-ln", "max_simulated")), big.mark = ",")`
moths against `r format(dist_sum$max_observed, big.mark = ",")` observed,
where NB2 simulates
`r format(round(dist_get("nbinom2", "max_simulated")), big.mark = ",")`.

Both statements can hold at once because a lognormal mixture this wide is
extremely right-skewed: most nights sit near its median, which is what the
likelihood rewards, while its mean and variance are carried by rare enormous
nights that the data do not contain.

## The answer, and what it is for

- For **describing or predicting nightly catches** — regression, prediction
  intervals, simulation — the **negative binomial (NB2)** is the distribution
  best adapted to these data: variance
  `r sprintf("%.1f", nb2_factor)` times the squared mean on top of the
  Poisson term, matching the empirical variance-mean relation across three
  orders of magnitude, with the better-behaved upper tail.
- The **Poisson-lognormal** is the better *description of the bulk* and the
  more interpretable mechanism — nightly catchability as a multiplicative
  random factor — but its second moment and tail are wrong, so it should not
  be used to simulate extremes.
- **Do not zero-inflate.** The empty nights need no separate mechanism.
- Neither family should be trusted for extreme quantiles: both overstate the
  largest catches.

Whichever is used, the size of the nightly term is the finding worth carrying
forward. A standard deviation of the nightly multiplier of
`r sprintf("%.1f", 1 / sqrt(dist_get("nbinom2", "dispersion")))` times the
mean under NB2 — an order of magnitude in each direction under the lognormal —
dwarfs everything the development models disagree about: a ten-day error in
the modelled median changes a given night's expected catch by less than the
night-to-night noise. It also explains the shape of these curves directly. A
third of a season's catch arriving on its single best night (@sec-lag) is not
a curious feature of spruce budworm flight; it is what a nightly multiplier of
this size produces on a seasonal curve of ordinary width.

One caveat on the fitting. `glmmTMB` warns that it was built against a
different version of `TMB` than the one installed here. The two leading fits
were therefore repeated with `lme4` — the Poisson-lognormal as an
observation-level random effect, the negative binomial through `glmer.nb` —
which reproduced the log-likelihoods to within 3 AIC and the nightly standard
deviation to three decimals, so the ranking does not rest on that warning.


# Forecasting from what a forecast has {#sec-forecast}

```{r}
#| label: forecast-data
timing <- readRDS(file.path("data", "processed", "flight_timing.rds"))
tim_scores <- timing$scores
tim_width  <- timing$width_summary
tim_cv     <- timing$cv
tim_sum    <- timing$summary

## Inline `r` cannot carry escaped backticks, so column lookups go through
## these helpers instead of backtick-quoted names.
tim_get <- function(sp, col) tim_scores[[col]][tim_scores$spec == sp]
tim_w   <- function(sp, col) tim_width[[col]][tim_width$spec == sp]
```

The sections above ask what the models get right. This one fixes the inputs a
forecast would actually have for a locality-year and asks how well the flight
season can be predicted from them:

1. a distribution of developmental dates — **pupation** from bayessbw, or
   **adult emergence** from BioSIM;
2. **hourly temperature** at the locality;
3. the season's **total catch**.

No trap data from the year being predicted. The season total being an input is
what makes this tractable: abundance is not modelled, only the share of that
total falling on each night.

## The distribution of adult dates

BioSIM's `Adults` column, kept in @sec-biosim, is a stock — it re-counts the
same individuals every day and sums to about 1,500% of the cohort, so it is
not a distribution. The series that is one is **`MaleEmergence +
FemaleEmergence`**, which sums to exactly 100%. At the regional point in 1978
it is centred on day 190.4 with a central 90% of 13.2 days, against 194.7 and
14.4 days for the flight curve: emergence is four days earlier and slightly
narrower, as it should be. This section is the first use of it.

## Nightly temperature

Flight is crepuscular, so temperature is averaged over the hours 20:00 to
02:00 of each trap-night, with the hours after midnight assigned to the night
that began the previous evening. Every one of the
`r format(tim_sum$n_nights, big.mark = ",")` trapped nights has a complete
window.

## Timing and nightly skill

```{r}
#| label: tbl-forecast
#| tbl-cap: "Leave-one-year-out skill from forecast inputs only. `+ temp` adds the nightly flight-hour temperature as a quadratic. All specifications are negative binomial with a locality-year level, so the season total is conditioned on rather than predicted"
tim_scores |>
  transmute(Specification = spec,
            `median error, d` = round(`median error, d`, 2),
            `RMSE, d` = round(`RMSE median, d`, 2),
            `log score per moth` = round(`log score per moth`, 3),
            `90% coverage` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * `90% coverage`)) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

**For the median date, the two BioSIM series are interchangeable and better
than bayessbw.** The flight curve gives
`r sprintf("%.2f", tim_get("flight (R/10 best)", "median error, d"))`
days of mean absolute error and emergence
`r sprintf("%.2f", tim_get("emergence", "median error, d"))`
— a difference of a sixth of a day, so **either BioSIM input can be used**.
Pupation from bayessbw costs about a day
(`r sprintf("%.2f", tim_get("pupation", "median error, d"))` d),
and a seasonal spline with temperature but no development model at all is no
better (`r sprintf("%.2f", tim_get("temperature only", "median error, d"))` d).

**Nightly temperature does not help the median, but it is the first thing that
has improved the nightly numbers.** Adding it moves the median error the wrong
way by a tenth of a day, while the log score per moth improves from
`r sprintf("%.3f", tim_get("flight (R/10 best)", "log score per moth"))`
to `r sprintf("%.3f", tim_get("flight + temp", "log score per moth"))`
with the flight curve and from
`r sprintf("%.3f", tim_get("emergence", "log score per moth"))`
to `r sprintf("%.3f", tim_get("emergence + temp", "log score per moth"))`
with emergence. Temperature decides **which nights inside the season** the
moths fly, not where the season sits — which is what the phenology is for.

## The predicted season is genuinely too wide

Earlier sections compared the predicted mean curve's central 90% with the
observed one and called the prediction over-dispersed. That comparison is not
quite fair: the observed width is measured on a single realisation of a very
overdispersed count, and a spiky realisation is narrower than the smooth mean
curve behind it. The check below simulates realisations from each fitted
predictive distribution and measures their widths exactly as the observed
width is measured.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-forecast-width
#| tbl-cap: "Central 90% of the flight season: the smooth mean curve, a simulated realisation of it (100 draws per locality-year), and the observed value. The last column is the share of locality-years whose observed width falls inside the simulated 90% band"
tim_width |>
  transmute(Specification = spec,
            `mean curve, d` = round(`mean-curve width, d`, 1),
            `realisation, d` = round(`simulated width, d`, 1),
            `observed, d` = round(`observed width, d`, 1),
            `inside the band` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * `inside the 90% band`)) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Sampling noise accounts for about a day of the gap — the mean curve of the
best specification spans
`r sprintf("%.1f", tim_w("flight + temp", "mean-curve width, d"))`
days and its realisations
`r sprintf("%.1f", tim_w("flight + temp", "simulated width, d"))`
— but the observed `r sprintf("%.1f", tim_sum$obs_width)` days is still about
two and a half days narrower than that, and only
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * tim_w("flight + temp", "inside the 90% band"))`
of locality-years fall inside the simulated band where 90% should. So the
over-width is real, and smaller than the figure quoted in @sec-count: the
honest statement is a realisation of
`r sprintf("%.1f", tim_w("flight + temp", "simulated width, d"))`
days against `r sprintf("%.1f", tim_sum$obs_width)` observed, not the mean
curve's `r sprintf("%.1f", tim_w("flight + temp", "mean-curve width, d"))`.

The nightly predictive intervals are correspondingly conservative: the 90%
negative binomial interval, with the season total supplied, contains the
observed count on
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * tim_get("flight + temp", "90% coverage"))`
of nights.

## Where this leaves the forecast

| Component | Best available | Skill |
|-----------|----------------|-------|
| Median flight date | BioSIM flight or emergence curve, calibrated | `r sprintf("%.1f", tim_scores[["median error, d"]][1])` d mean absolute error, out of sample |
| Which nights within the season | the same, plus nightly flight-hour temperature | log score per moth `r sprintf("%.3f", tim_get("flight + temp", "log score per moth"))` against `r sprintf("%.3f", tim_get("flight (R/10 best)", "log score per moth"))` without it |
| Count on a given night | negative binomial, θ from @sec-dist, mean = share × season total | 90% interval covers `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * tim_get("flight + temp", "90% coverage"))` of nights |
| Season width | all specifications too broad by about 2.5 d | `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * tim_width[["inside the 90% band"]][1])` of observed widths inside the simulated band |

: The forecast as it stands {#tbl-forecast-summary}

The one clear deficiency is the width. Every driver produces a season two to
five days too broad, and the ranking of drivers by width follows their ranking
by timing, which suggests a common cause: the shape correction is fitted
across all locality-years and cannot know that a particular season will be
compressed. A scale parameter on the fitted shape — sharpening the predicted
curve by a factor estimated out of sample — is the obvious next step and has
not been tried.


# A callable predictor {#sec-predictor}

```{r}
#| label: predictor-data
predictor <- readRDS(file.path("data", "processed", "flight_predictor.rds"))
pred_cal  <- predictor$calibration
pred_mod  <- predictor$models

pcal <- function(dr, cr, col) {
  pred_cal[[col]][pred_cal$driver == dr & pred_cal$criterion == cr]
}
```

`R/13_fit_flight_predictor.R` fits the model on every year and stores what is
needed to predict a locality-year that was never trapped;
`R/functions/predict_flight.R` consumes it. The call takes the three forecast
inputs and nothing else:

```r
source("R/functions/predict_flight.R")

out <- predict_flight(
  dev_curve    = emergence_1978,   # data frame: doy, pct
  hourly_temp  = weather_1978,     # data frame: datetime, Temp
  season_total = 12000,            # moths caught that season
  driver       = "emergence"       # or "flight", or "pupation"
)
```

It returns one row per night: the share of the season expected that night, the
expected count, and a negative binomial predictive interval. Three driver
variants are stored, so whichever developmental distribution is to hand can be
used — BioSIM's flight or emergence curve, or bayessbw's pupation
distribution.

The shares are normalised over the nights supplied, so the answer is always
*of this season's catch, how much falls on each of these nights*. A window
shorter than the flight season inflates every share, exactly as a trap that
operates for part of the season does.

## Sharpening, and the trade-off it forces

@sec-forecast leaves the predicted season two to five days too broad. The
fitted shape is a log-share curve, so raising it to a power κ > 1 sharpens it
around its own peak without moving the peak. κ is chosen out of sample by
stacking: for each year it is the value that scores best on the *other* years'
held-out predictions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictor-kappa
#| tbl-cap: "Held-out skill with and without sharpening. `logscore` chooses the sharpening that maximises the nightly log score; `width` chooses the one that makes the predicted season the right length"
## Column names are set afterwards: R rejects \u escapes inside
## backtick-quoted names.
pred_cal |>
  mutate(criterion = recode(criterion, none = "none",
                            logscore = "by log score", width = "by width")) |>
  transmute(driver, criterion, kappa = round(kappa, 2),
            med = round(`median error, d`, 2),
            wid = sprintf("%+.2f", `width error, d`),
            ls  = round(`log score per moth`, 3)) |>
  setNames(c("Driver", "\u03ba chosen", "\u03ba", "median error, d",
             "width error, d", "log score per moth")) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

The two criteria disagree, and the disagreement is the useful part.

**By the log score, no sharpening at all.** κ = 1 for every driver: the proper
scoring rule for nightly counts prefers the broad curve, because sharpening
moves mass away from the shoulders where a handful of moths still arrive, and
the log score punishes that heavily.

**By width, κ between
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(pred_cal$kappa[pred_cal$criterion == "width"]))` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(pred_cal$kappa[pred_cal$criterion == "width"]))`**, and
it works almost exactly: with the flight curve the width error falls from
`r sprintf("%+.2f", pcal("flight", "none", "width error, d"))` days to
`r sprintf("%+.2f", pcal("flight", "width", "width error, d"))` days. The cost
is a tenth of a day on the median
(`r sprintf("%.2f", pcal("flight", "none", "median error, d"))` →
`r sprintf("%.2f", pcal("flight", "width", "median error, d"))`) and
`r sprintf("%.3f", pcal("flight", "none", "log score per moth") - pcal("flight", "width", "log score per moth"))`
on the log score per moth.

So the choice depends on the use. For **when to expect flight and over what
window** — the operational question — sharpen: the season comes out the right
length at a negligible cost in the median. For **probabilistic statements
about a particular night's count**, leave κ = 1. `predict_flight()` defaults to
the sharpened setting and takes `kappa = "logscore"` or a number to override.

## A worked example

```{r}
#| label: fig-predictor
#| fig-cap: "Two locality-years predicted from their emergence curve, hourly temperature and season total, with the sharpened shape. Line: expected catch. Band: 90% negative binomial interval. Points: the observed catches, which the model never saw for these years. Counts are plotted plus one on a log scale."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
source(file.path("R", "functions", "predict_flight.R"))
library(ggplot2)

wx_all <- readRDS(file.path("data", "processed", "weather_hourly.rds"))

one_case <- function(loc, yr) {
  obs <- timing$dat |> filter(Location == loc, Year == yr) |> arrange(doy)
  emerg <- timing$regional_emergence |> filter(Year == yr) |>
    transmute(doy, pct = emergence)
  wx <- wx_all |> filter(Location == loc, Year == yr) |> pull(Weather) |>
    first() |> transmute(datetime = datetime_est, Temp)
  p <- predict_flight(emerg, wx, sum(obs$moths), driver = "emergence",
                      nights_doy = obs$doy, kappa = "width")
  left_join(p, select(obs, doy, observed = moths), by = "doy") |>
    mutate(panel = sprintf("%s  %d", sub(", Maine$", "", loc), yr))
}

cases <- bind_rows(
  one_case("East Allagash Twp. (St. Francis), T17 R11, Maine", 1983),
  one_case("Meddybemps Township, Maine", 1981)
)

## Median error of each panel, for the text below.
med_of <- function(doy, v) {
  keep <- v > 0
  cum <- cumsum(v[keep]) / sum(v[keep])
  stats::approx(c(0, cum), c(min(doy[keep]) - 1, doy[keep]),
                xout = 0.5, ties = "ordered")$y
}
case_err <- cases |>
  group_by(panel) |>
  summarise(total = sum(observed),
            err = med_of(doy, share) - med_of(doy, observed),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(cases, aes(doy)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower + 1, ymax = upper + 1), fill = "#1f6f8b",
              alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(aes(y = expected + 1), colour = "#1f6f8b", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed + 1), colour = "grey20", size = 1.5) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Day of year", y = "Moths per night + 1") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The left panel is the largest catch in the dataset,
`r format(case_err$total[1], big.mark = ",")` moths over
`r sum(cases$panel == case_err$panel[1])` nights; its median is predicted
`r sprintf("%+.1f", case_err$err[1])` days out, and the right panel's
`r sprintf("%+.1f", case_err$err[2])` days. The
temperature term is visible in both: the sharp dips are cold nights, and the
observed catches dip with them — day 187 at East Allagash averaged 6.9 °C
through the flight hours and caught one moth, where the neighbouring warm
nights caught hundreds.

The intervals are wide, and honestly so: with θ =
`r sprintf("%.2f", pred_mod$emergence$theta)` a night expected to yield a
thousand moths has a 90% interval running from a few dozen to several
thousand. That is the nightly variability measured in @sec-dist, not a defect
of the phenology.

## What it does not do

- It does not predict **abundance**: the season total is an input. Predicting
  that needs a population model, which nothing in this project provides.
- It has no **site term**, by design — @sec-regional showed site-specific
  weather makes the timing worse, and every latitude term tried has hurt.
- It inherits the **southern excess** of @sec-count: localities below 45.5 °N
  are fitted about a day worse than northern ones.
- Its inputs must be **regional**: the fitted variants use BioSIM run once at
  the network centroid. Feeding it a curve from a site-specific run is a
  different input from the one it was calibrated on.


# The missing nights are censoring {#sec-censor}

```{r}
#| label: censor-data
cens      <- readRDS(file.path("data", "processed", "censoring_check.rds"))
cens_rows <- cens$rows
cs        <- cens$summary

cget <- function(q, col) cs$headline[[col]][cs$headline$quantity == q]

## Per-record lookups, so the text below carries no transcribed numbers.
crow <- function(id, col) cens_rows[[col]][cens_rows$flightID == id]
n_comparable <- sum(readRDS(file.path("data", "processed",
                                      "model_vs_observed.rds"))$comparable)
```

An `m` night is not a night whose catch is unknown in the way a lottery number
is unknown. It is a night inside a running trapping period whose catch was not
recorded, and because flight is a seasonal curve, where the night falls decides
which part of that curve is unidentified. `R/01_read_trap_data.R` therefore
reads them as **censoring**: a missing night before 15 July bounds the rise of
the season (left-censored), a missing night after it bounds the decline
(right-censored). The side is carried on every night in `trap_daily$censoring`
and counted per record in `n_cens_left` / `n_cens_right`.

Of the `r cs$n_cens_nights` missing nights in the working dataset,
`r cs$n_left` are left-censored and `r cs$n_right` right-censored, spread over
`r cs$n_records` records. A further `r cs$n_excluded` record was removed from
the dataset because of where its censored nights fell (below).

## The side is not the magnitude

A censored night costs what the season was doing on it, and those two blocks
of twelve mid-June nights in 1983 cost nothing at all — nothing was flying.
`R/14_censoring.R` makes that quantitative: for each affected record the
fitted predictor (@sec-predictor) is given the record's own night set, counted
and censored together, and asked how much of the season it expects on the
nights with no count. The percentiles are then re-estimated with those nights
completed at their expected level, and the difference is the bias that
treating a censored night as simply absent introduces.

The distribution is extremely skewed. Across the records retained in the
dataset the median has `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * cs$median_share)` of its
season inside censored nights, and only `r cs$n_material` of
`r cs$n_assessed` assessed records exceed
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cs$material_cut)`, the largest reaching
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * cs$max_share)`. One record was far outside that
range and was excluded on the strength of it (below).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-censor
#| tbl-cap: "The records where censoring is material: more than 1% of the season expected on nights with no count. `shift` is how far the percentile moves when the censored nights are completed at their expected level"
cens_rows |>
  filter(is_material, !excluded) |>
  transmute(Record = sub(", Maine$", "", locality), Year = year,
            side, nights = n_cens_left + n_cens_right,
            `DOY` = sprintf("%d-%d", cens_doy_lo, cens_doy_hi),
            `season total` = season_total,
            `censored` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * cens_share),
            `implied extra moths` = round(implied_extra),
            `shift p50, d` = sprintf("%+.1f", d_p50),
            `shift p95, d` = sprintf("%+.1f", d_p95)) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

One record was removed from the dataset rather than flagged. Elliotsville
Township in 1978 has only two censored nights — 8 and 9 July — but they sit at
the peak, and the predictor expects
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * crow(509, "cens_share"))` of the whole season on
them: `r format(round(crow(509, "implied_extra")), big.mark = ",")` moths
against the `r format(crow(509, "season_total"), big.mark = ",")` recorded.
Completing them moves its median catch date
`r sprintf("%+.1f", crow(509, "d_p50"))` days and p95
`r sprintf("%+.1f", crow(509, "d_p95"))` days. That is not a flight curve with
a gap in it but one missing its peak, so no percentile taken from it is
identifiable, and `exclude_records` in `R/01_read_trap_data.R` drops it. Its
nights are kept in `data/processed/trap_excluded.rds` so this diagnostic — the
one that justified the decision — still reports it.

The record passed `usable_phenology` and `flight_complete` throughout, because
neither flag looks at *where* a gap falls relative to the catch. That is a
limitation of those flags: a censored peak is invisible to them.

The two right-censored 1983 records behave as expected for a gap in the
declining tail: Hay Lake's p95 moves
`r sprintf("%+.1f", crow(608, "d_p95"))` days with the
median untouched. Steuben 1989 is the smallest season in the group
(`r crow(735, "season_total")` moths) and its five late-June nights shift the
median `r sprintf("%+.1f", crow(735, "d_p50"))` days.

One record could not be assessed: Meddybemps Township in 1987 has no regional
emergence curve, 1987 being one of the three years with no comparable
locality-year.

## The published aggregates do not move

```{r}
#| label: tbl-censor-headline
#| tbl-cap: "The two headline spatial numbers, recomputed with every affected record's percentiles completed"
cens$headline |>
  transmute(Quantity = quantity,
            `As published` = sprintf("%+.2f", published),
            `Censoring completed` = sprintf("%+.2f", completed)) |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r"))
```

The median model-observation offset is unchanged at
`r sprintf("%+.2f", cget("median offset, d", "completed"))` days and the
observed latitudinal gradient moves from
`r sprintf("%+.3f", cget("observed gradient, d per degree N", "published"))` to
`r sprintf("%+.3f", cget("observed gradient, d per degree N", "completed"))`
days per degree north. Three materially affected records out of
`r n_comparable` cannot move a median, and the gradient conclusion of
@sec-sync survives untouched.

So the censoring rule changes no result reported here. What it changes is what
may be done next: a record whose peak is censored should not contribute to a
width or late-tail analysis at face value, and `censoring` now makes those
records findable instead of leaving them indistinguishable from complete ones.
The diagnostic is deliberately not a correction — nothing downstream reads the
completed percentiles.


# Findings so far {#sec-summary}

```{r}
#| label: summary-data
## Everything here is taken from the objects loaded by the sections above, so
## the summary cannot drift from the analysis it summarises.
sy <- list(
  records    = nrow(trap_records),
  localities = n_distinct(trap_records$locality),
  years      = n_distinct(trap_records$year),
  yr_from    = min(trap_records$year),
  yr_to      = max(trap_records$year),
  nights     = sum(trap_daily$status == "counted"),
  usable     = sum(trap_records$usable_phenology),
  comparable = nrow(cmp),
  hours      = sum(vapply(weather_hourly$Weather, nrow, integer(1))),
  complete   = sum(biosim_flight$flight_complete),
  bio_p50    = mean(biosim_flight$p50),
  pup_p50    = mean(pupal_phenology$p50),
  pup_spread = mean(pupal_phenology$spread),
  pup_post   = mean(pupal_phenology$post_hi - pupal_phenology$post_lo),
  off_p50    = median(cmp$d_p50),
  off_p05    = median(cmp$d_p05),
  off_p95    = median(cmp$d_p95),
  lag_bayes  = median(cmp$lag_bayes),
  lag_biosim = median(cmp$lag_biosim),
  r_year     = with(cmp |> group_by(Year) |> filter(n() >= 5) |>
                      summarise(s = mean(sim_p50), o = mean(obs_p50),
                                .groups = "drop"), cor(s, o)),
  r_within   = cor(residuals(lm(sim_p50 ~ factor(Year), cmp)),
                   residuals(lm(obs_p50 ~ factor(Year), cmp))),
  r_models   = cor(cmp$d_p50, cmp$d_p50_bayes)
)
```

## The data

`r sy$records` Maine light-trap records from the Rhainds compilation cover
`r sy$localities` localities and `r sy$years` years
(`r sy$yr_from`–`r sy$yr_to`), with
`r format(sy$nights, big.mark = ",")` counted trap-nights, every record above
99 moths for the season. The minimum-effort rule of @sec-traps marks
`r sy$usable` records as usable for percentile phenology; intersected with the
modelled cohorts that finish flight, **`r sy$comparable` locality-years** carry
a meaningful model-versus-observed comparison. Hourly CaSR weather was
extracted for all `r sy$records` locality-years
(`r format(round(sy$hours / 1e6, 2), nsmall = 2)` million hours).

## Two development models that agree with each other

BioSIM's `Spruce_Budworm_Biology` and the Bayesian model of bayessbw were
fitted to different data, by different methods, and were driven by different
weather — BioSIM's own station network against the CaSR grid. They place
pupation within a day of each other (@tbl-pupal-vs-biosim), and both put the
observed median catch about a fortnight after predicted pupation
(`r sprintf("%.1f", sy$lag_bayes)` d for bayessbw,
`r sprintf("%.1f", sy$lag_biosim)` d for BioSIM). In the pupation model,
individual variation exceeds parameter uncertainty about fourfold: a
population takes `r sprintf("%.1f", sy$pup_spread)` days to pupate from p05 to
p95, while the posterior places its median to within
`r sprintf("%.1f", sy$pup_post)` days.

## The central finding

Against the catches, modelled flight is early by a median
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(sy$off_p50))` days at p50
(`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(sy$off_p05))` d at p05,
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(sy$off_p95))` d at p95). That average hides a split:
year means correlate at `r sprintf("%.2f", sy$r_year)`, but within a year
across localities the correlation is `r sprintf("%.2f", sy$r_within)`.

The reason is a **gradient-slope error**. Both models spread flight across
Maine about seven times more steeply with latitude than the catches do
(@tbl-sync-gradient): `r sprintf("%+.2f", sync_grad$d_per_degree[1])` days per
degree observed, against `r sprintf("%+.2f", sync_grad$d_per_degree[2])`
(BioSIM) and `r sprintf("%+.2f", sync_grad$d_per_degree[3])` (bayessbw) — 
`r sprintf("%.1f", sync_sum$obs_spread)` days of observed spread across the
network against `r sprintf("%.1f", sync_sum$sim_spread)` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", sync_sum$bayes_spread)` modelled. Flight in Maine is
essentially synchronous, and the apparent "early in the south" offset is the
difference between a steep modelled gradient and a flat real one. The two
models' offsets correlate at `r sprintf("%.2f", sy$r_models)`, locality-year
by locality-year, which is why the same error appears in both.

## Five explanations tested and set aside

| Candidate | Evidence against it | Where |
|-----------|---------------------|-------|
| The weather source | both models make the same spatial error on different weather (offsets correlate `r sprintf("%.2f", sy$r_models)`) | @sec-compare |
| A temperature-driven pupal stage | degree-days beat a constant lag by `r sprintf("%.2f", lag_sum$cv_rmse_A - lag_sum$cv_rmse_B)` d out of sample; the interval's correlation with post-pupation temperature is `r sprintf("%+.2f", lag_sum$r_lag_tpost)` and a spline on it reaches R² `r sprintf("%.3f", lag_sum$spline_r2)`; `r sprintf("%.0f%%", lag_sum$var_share[1])` of its variance is between localities | @sec-lag |
| Elevation and topography | all `r elev_sum$n_localities` elevations measured (`r sprintf("%.0f", elev_sum$elev_range[1])`–`r sprintf("%.0f", elev_sum$elev_range[2])` m); supplying them shifts flight `r sprintf("%+.1f", elev_sum$mean_shift)` d and leaves the gradient at `r sprintf("%+.1f", elev_sum$grad_usgs)` d per degree | @sec-elev |
| A detection threshold at low catch | small catches carry *more* of their catch after the modelled window and have slightly wider curves — the opposite of clipping | @sec-compare |
| Nightly-scale immigration | `r sync_sum$n_pairs` within-year locality pairs give a median nightly correlation of `r sprintf("%.2f", sync_sum$r0_median)` against a shuffled-year null of `r sprintf("%.2f", sync_sum$null_median)`, decaying with distance, weakest north–south, at zero lag | @sec-sync |

: What the residual is not {#tbl-summary-ruled-out}

Catch size survives as a second, weaker and near-independent site covariate:
`r sprintf("%+.2f", coef(lm(d_p50 ~ Latitude + log10(season_total), cmp))[["log10(season_total)"]])`
days per tenfold catch against
`r sprintf("%+.2f", coef(lm(d_p50 ~ Latitude + log10(season_total), cmp))[["Latitude"]])`
days per degree of latitude, and with no effect within a locality.

## What predicts the flight season

Site-specific weather makes both models worse than a single regional series
(@tbl-regional). Built into the nightly count model of @sec-count, the
calibrated regional curve predicts a held-out year's median catch date to
`r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best$mae)` days of mean absolute error, bias
`r sprintf("%+.2f", cnt_best$bias)` d, with
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cnt_best$within)` of locality-years inside five
days — against `r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$mae[cnt_best_all$model == "clim"])`
days for a seasonal climatology.

Two qualifications matter for using it. First, the development model
contributes **the date, not the shape**: with an exponent of
`r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_sum$exponent)` on the modelled curve, deleting the
curve entirely and keeping only its median plus the empirical correction costs
nothing on timing (`r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$mae[cnt_best_all$model == "reg-med"])`
days). BioSIM's uncorrected site curve, meanwhile, buys nothing over
climatology — it ties on mean absolute error and is worse on RMSE, on the
nightly likelihood and on bias. Second, the calibrated prediction is
**over-dispersed**: it widens the predicted central 90% to
`r sprintf("%.1f", cnt_sum$cal_width)` days against
`r sprintf("%.1f", cnt_sum$obs_width)` observed, so an interval read straight
off the fitted curve is conservative.

The distribution around that prediction is also settled (@sec-dist): a night's
catch is **negative binomial** with a variance about
`r sprintf("%.1f", 1 / dist_cmp$dispersion[dist_cmp$family == "nbinom2"])`
times the squared mean, it needs no zero inflation, and the implied
night-to-night multiplier varies by an order of magnitude in each direction —
more than anything the development models disagree about.

bayessbw's pupation distribution does not improve on this
(`r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$mae[cnt_best_all$model == "pup+"])` d
site-specific, `r sprintf("%.2f", cnt_best_all$mae[cnt_best_all$model == "pupreg+"])` d
regional). Its value in this project is as the independent check on pupation
timing, not as the driver of the prediction.

## A predictor that can be called

`predict_flight()` (@sec-predictor) packages the result into the three inputs
that will be available at prediction time: a developmental distribution, hourly
temperature, and the season total. On held-out years it places the median
catch date within about three days and, with the sharpening parameter set by
width, returns a season of the right length. It predicts shares of a given
total, never the total itself.

## What is still open

- **Wind and precipitation are still unused.** Nightly temperature is now in
  the model (@sec-forecast) and it is the one covariate that improves the
  nightly numbers, but it does not move the median; wind and precipitation are
  already extracted per locality-night and would enter the same way.
- **Immigration is not excluded, only unsupported at the nightly scale.**
  Arrivals need not be simultaneous across localities, and no systematic
  search for second modes has been made across the `r sy$comparable` curves.
  Millinocket in 1980 (@fig-catch-shape) is the one panel that looks like an
  influx.
- **The southern excess survives calibration.** The count model's residual
  correlates only `r sprintf("%+.2f", cor(cnt_cv$err_p50[cnt_cv$model == "reg+"], cnt_nights$Latitude[match(cnt_cv$site_year[cnt_cv$model == "reg+"], cnt_nights$site_year)]))`
  with latitude, but southern localities are still fitted about a day worse
  than northern ones, so the gradient is corrected on average rather than
  explained.
- **Abundance is not modelled at all.** Every result here is about timing; the
  season total is an input to the predictive model, never an output.
